package_info.package_manager: N/A (custom Windows malware, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.package_versions: Current version as used by LuoYu APT
package_info.why_malicious: WinDealer is a sophisticated information stealer and backdoor malware attributed to the LuoYu APT group. It is distributed via malicious automatic updates of legitimate Windows applications. Once installed, it enables attackers to search for and exfiltrate sensitive data, establish persistent backdoor access for remote command execution, manipulate files, and propagate laterally within networks. Its primary objectives are unauthorized data theft, persistent system compromise, and facilitating further attacks.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (post-compromise, after malware installation via fake update)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into legitimate application process memory or dropped as a separate executable in the application update directory
required_permissions: filesystem (read access to user and system files)
process_execution (to run within or alongside legitimate processes)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker-controlled code recursively enumerates files and directories on the infected system, collects files matching sensitive patterns (e.g., documents, credentials), and transmits the collected data to a remote command-and-control (C2) server over HTTP/S.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ (typical for Windows malware, exact language not specified in report)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-compromise), the code recursively enumerates files and directories, collects files matching sensitive patterns, and transmits the collected data to a remote C2 server over HTTP/S, resulting in unauthorized data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated, recursive file enumeration and exfiltration of user and system data to an external, attacker-controlled server is a hallmark of infostealer malware and is not a behavior exhibited by legitimate software updates.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software updates should not access or transmit user files to unknown remote servers, nor should they perform broad file system searches outside their own update context.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise backup or remote support tools may transmit user data, but only to trusted, documented endpoints and with explicit user consent and logging.
key_indicators: Automated recursive file and directory enumeration
Collection of files matching sensitive patterns (e.g., *.doc, *.xls, credential files)
Outbound HTTP/S connections to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure
Data exfiltration following application update events

execution_context.trigger: runtime (post-compromise, after initial infection and data exfiltration)
execution_context.file_location: Injected into legitimate application process or installed as a persistent Windows service (e.g., via new service creation or autostart registry modification)
required_permissions: filesystem (write access to registry or service configuration)
process_execution (to spawn or inject into processes)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malware establishes persistence by registering itself as a Windows service or modifying autostart registry keys, then opens a network socket to listen for remote commands from the attacker's C2 server, enabling arbitrary command execution on the infected system.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ (typical for Windows malware, exact language not specified in report)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-compromise), the code creates or modifies persistence mechanisms (such as Windows services or autostart registry keys), establishes a network connection to the C2 server, and listens for remote commands, enabling the attacker to execute arbitrary commands and maintain ongoing control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Establishing unauthorized persistence and enabling remote command execution are core malicious activities that provide attackers with ongoing, covert access to the compromised system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not create persistence mechanisms or allow remote command execution without explicit user knowledge, consent, and security controls.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools (RATs) and IT management software may implement similar features, but only with explicit user consent, strong authentication, and audit logging.
key_indicators: Creation or modification of Windows services or autostart registry keys without user consent
Network socket listening for inbound commands from external C2 infrastructure
Execution of arbitrary system commands received from remote server
Persistence established outside normal application update mechanisms

execution_context.file_location: Injected into legitimate application process or loaded as a separate module in the system or network share directories
required_permissions: network (to access other systems for lateral movement)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malware manipulates files by modifying, deleting, or creating new files on the local system and attempts to propagate itself to other systems on the local network by copying its payload to accessible network shares or exploiting vulnerabilities for lateral movement.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ (typical for Windows malware, exact language not specified in report)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-compromise), the code modifies, deletes, or creates files on the local system, then attempts to propagate itself to other systems on the network by copying its payload to network shares or exploiting network vulnerabilities, resulting in lateral movement and further compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unauthorized file manipulation and self-propagation across networked systems are classic malware behaviors used to spread infection, evade detection, and maintain attacker control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software updates should not modify unrelated files or attempt to spread themselves to other systems without explicit user action and proper authentication.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise deployment tools may propagate updates or modify files, but only with proper authentication, user awareness, and within defined operational boundaries.
key_indicators: Unauthorized modification, deletion, or creation of files outside update scope
Copying of malware payload to network shares or remote systems
Network-based propagation attempts (e.g., exploiting SMB or RDP vulnerabilities)
Lateral movement activity following initial infection

attack_chain.action: Malware is delivered via malicious automatic updates of legitimate applications, resulting in initial infection of the target system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the WinDealer malicious payload on the victim system

attack_chain.action: Malware searches for and collects sensitive data from the infected system using automated file enumeration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive data to attacker-controlled infrastructure

attack_chain.action: Malware establishes persistence and backdoor access by creating or modifying Windows services or autostart registry entries, and connects to the C2 server to await remote commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can issue remote commands and maintain persistent access to the compromised system

attack_chain.action: Malware manipulates files on the local system and attempts to propagate itself to other systems on the network via network shares or exploitation of vulnerabilities.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential lateral movement and further compromise of additional systems

behavioral_signatures: Automated recursive file and directory enumeration followed by outbound data transfer to unknown remote servers
Creation or modification of unauthorized Windows services or autostart registry entries for persistence
Establishment of network connections to external C2 infrastructure and listening for remote command execution
Unauthorized modification, deletion, or creation of files outside the application's normal update scope
Propagation attempts to other systems on the local network via network shares or exploitation of SMB/RDP vulnerabilities
file_indicators: Unexpected executables or DLLs present in application update directories (e.g., C:\Program Files\<AppName>\Update\)
New or modified autostart registry entries (e.g., HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) or scheduled tasks
Files with anomalous names or locations mimicking legitimate application files
Presence of dropped payloads in network share directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections to attacker-controlled C2 domains or IP addresses as specified in the report
Unusual HTTP/S traffic patterns immediately following application update events
Beaconing behavior to dynamic or previously unseen domains not associated with the legitimate application
Network traffic indicative of lateral movement (e.g., SMB, RDP, or RPC connections to peer systems)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for automated file enumeration and outbound data transfers following application updates, creation or modification of unauthorized Windows services, autostart registry entries, or scheduled tasks, and outbound connections to suspicious or previously unknown domains or IPs. Correlate process creation and network activity with update processes to identify injected or dropped malware components. Use behavioral analysis to detect remote command execution, unauthorized file manipulation, and lateral movement attempts across the network. Implement alerting for the presence of unexpected executables or DLLs in update directories and anomalous registry or scheduled task modifications.
